svg.text: The origin, and the strata of defence piled on it
The same-origin policy blocks "reads" and not "sends". Everything else derives from that asymmetry.
origin = scheme + host + port
baseline: https://example.com:443/app
Cookies do not use this criterion – they judge by domain and path, ignoring port.
The basic unit being split in two is the starting point of many problems at this layer.
The asymmetry of the same-origin policy
Blocked – reads
DOM access to another origin's document
reading response bodies · reading cookies
Not blocked – sends
requests via img · form · script tags,
with the cookies attached
Even unable to read the response, the request already reached the server and was processed.
→ CSRF is this asymmetry itself, not an implementation mistake.
The path of observing only differences in response without reading (XS-Leaks) lives in the same gap.
The defences added since – each a response to a particular incident

g.text: Allows legitimate cross-origin API calls, with the server expressing permission in a response header.
reflecting the request's Origin + allowing credentials / trusting the null origin
On the premise that XSS will not go away, it limits where executable scripts come from to reduce the damage.
a JSONP endpoint inside the allow list · missing base-uri · library gadgets
Secure · HttpOnly · SameSite · the __Host- prefix. A belated correction for cookies not being origin-based.
SameSite=Lax still allows top-level GET · cookie injection from a subdomain
Specifies who may put my page in an iframe. The successor to X-Frame-Options.
clickjacking – luring the user's click over a transparent frame
Introduced after Spectre. A declaration not to put another origin's resources in the same process or group.
features such as SharedArrayBuffer open only to documents declaring isolation with these headers

svg.text: State partitioning – and where a plan was once withdrawn
Cache and storage were partitioned to include "within which site it is used" (answering cache probing and XS-Leaks). On the cookie side, partitioning remains as CHIPS.
But Chrome's third-party cookie deprecation was withdrawn in July 2024 and much of Privacy Sandbox was retired in 2025. Safari, Firefox and Brave still block them.
